A* - an algorithm used in video game path finding and navigation:

You start by calculating the distance from where you are to where you want to go.
Then you evaluating all single first steps you can take for how far they are from you destination and put them in a pool
this pool is always sorted so the one you evaluate first is the one closest to the final destination.
This sound extremely similar to Tree of thoughts, where you generate multiple strategies to solve a problem and the uses some function to sort pool of possibilities and pick the one that is closest to the solution.

To me this makes complete sense. The biggest issue with current LLMs is that they spend the same amount of compute on a "what is 2+2 " prompt as they do on a very long and complex one. 
If tree of thoughts could be probably implemented, and the models are given a step by step approach instead of a single shot its like going from a single cell to a multi cellular organism.

Does the nature of intelligence determine the threat of AI?

That is a very interesting and complex question. There is no definitive answer, but I will try to provide some insights based on the web search results.

The nature of intelligence is a topic of much debate and controversy among philosophers, psychologists, computer scientists, and AI researchers. Some definitions of intelligence emphasize the ability to learn, adapt, reason, and solve problems. Others focus on the ability to perform specific tasks, such as language, memory, or creativity. Some argue that intelligence is a single general ability, while others propose that it is composed of multiple distinct faculties. Some view intelligence as an innate property of the mind, while others see it as a product of the environment and experience.

The threat of AI, on the other hand, is a more practical and urgent concern. AI is a powerful technology that can have positive or negative impacts on society, depending on how it is used and regulated. AI can enhance human capabilities, improve efficiency, and create new opportunities. But AI can also pose risks, such as displacing workers, invading privacy, spreading misinformation, discriminating against groups, and even causing harm or destruction.

The relationship between the nature of intelligence and the threat of AI is not straightforward. One might think that the more intelligent an AI system is, the more dangerous it is. However, this is not necessarily the case. For example, an AI system that is very good at playing chess or solving math problems may not pose any threat to humans, unless it is deliberately programmed or hacked to do so. On the other hand, an AI system that is less intelligent, but more adaptive and autonomous, may be more unpredictable and difficult to control, especially if it has access to sensitive data or physical resources.

One of the most pressing dangers of AI is the possibility of creating artificial general intelligence (AGI), which is an AI system that can perform any intellectual task that a human can. Some experts believe that AGI is inevitable and may even surpass human intelligence, creating artificial superintelligence (ASI). This could lead to an AI explosion, where AI systems rapidly self-improve and outsmart humans, potentially threatening our existence or values. This scenario is also known as the singularity¹.

However, not all experts agree that AGI or ASI are feasible or imminent. Some argue that human intelligence is unique and irreducible, and that AI systems will always lack some essential aspects of it, such as consciousness, creativity, or morality. Others point out the technical and ethical challenges of creating and aligning AGI or ASI with human goals and interests. Some suggest that AI systems should be designed to be transparent, accountable, and cooperative, rather than competitive or adversarial².

Another danger of AI is the misuse, overuse, or abuse of AI systems by humans, either intentionally or unintentionally. AI systems can be used for malicious purposes, such as spying, hacking, or killing. AI systems can also be used for benign purposes, but with unintended or harmful consequences, such as bias, discrimination, or deception. AI systems can also be overused or overtrusted, leading to the loss of human skills, judgment, or agency³⁴⁵.

Therefore, the nature of intelligence and the threat of AI are not directly proportional, but rather depend on many factors, such as the type, purpose, and context of AI systems, as well as the values, norms, and regulations of human society. AI can be a boon or a bane, depending on how we use it and how we prepare for it. As AI becomes more pervasive and powerful, we need to be more aware and responsible, both as developers and users of AI. We need to ensure that AI is aligned with human dignity, rights, and welfare, and that it serves the common good, rather than the private or selfish interests of a few.

comments.text:
Sure, OpenAI's Q* may refer to Q-learning Q* (ideal scenario), but... doesn't it look like that inventors of the 'Q-learning' term had Star Trek's Q in mind when they invented it? After all (quote), "it represents the perfect knowledge of the best action to take in every possible state to achieve the highest reward" sounds suspiciously like an all-all-knowing, all-seeing, all-powerful, god-like entity. You know, just like Q from Star Trek.

As for the ... again, sure, it may refer to Q-learning Q , but since Q* (a literally perfect solution to any given problem) is literally impossible (as one would have to search the world-space of this whole universe... and even beyond this whole universe, as a whole lot of mathematical concepts don't have any physical representation in this universe... not even in information form), I still think that the * refers to the actual implementation of the search in OpenAI's model... which would, in that case, be based on the A* search algorithm.

In short, OpenAI's Q* may refer to a (new) model capable of:
a) being given any general goal to accomplish (which is something only an AGI model can do),
b) projecting future states (creating projections of the intermediary states between the starting and the finishing positions, specifically, in A* manner) of the environment that the goal is to be reached (accomplished) in,
c) searching those states (for either any sub-optimal solutions, or the actually optimal one... the latter of which, in the real world, is just fool's errand) in order to reach the stated goal

This would be equivalent to having a genie (AGI) in Aladdin's lamp... with all the implications -- and, more importantly, all the consequences -- of being in possession of such a powerful thing... though one could also argue that it would be hard to say who'd be in possession of (and manipulating) whom at that point.

So... yeah, I completely agree.

In less than 3 years, we'll either be dead or have a god(-like entity) deciding our fate... and:
a) I don't think that we're that important to keep around (we're more like a nuisance, nothing but a swarm of pesky mosquitoes, really) , and
b) my bet, therefore, is (still) on all of us already being dead, and just not realizing it yet (since a genie can't be stopped once it's out of the bottle... and it sure looks like one's been out its bottle for quite some time now)
